title: “STFU and build”: the body-of-work fight that matured
summary:
The most quotable move was @visakanv’s 2021 viral gut-punch: if you call yourself ambitious but can’t point to a body of work, “you should STFU and build the body of work first”—even if it’s “notes and drafts and crappy prototypes.” He doubles down that pretending is corrosive (“don’t try to steal valor”), then sharpens it into a social model: in a scene of 1,000, if 950 admit they’re not that serious, they can support the 50 “hell-bent on going the distance.”

That provocation is what triggered everything: some people felt called out, others felt relieved. @nobu_hibiki was the clearest counter-vibe—basically, “this made me accept I don’t have burning passion… I just want to go on with my life,” turning the thread into a permission slip for non-ambition (and a whole “tense like water / keep the water source clean” personal ethic spiral). The peak, though, was @AskYatharth flipping the argument into a public-vs-private distinction: he says his best move was stopping “vast annals of private unpublished notes” and putting them on Twitter, because unpublished work has personal value but “no public significance.” His metaphor—public significance “pushes against the dominoes”—became the intellectual upgrade from Visa’s blunt “prove it.”

After the dunking phase, the discourse mellowed into craft advice. @christineist lands the compromise line: “Make the best work you can, but if you cannot, making any work is better than making zero work,” plus “curate what you share.” @vincent_yc_li extends it into a community recipe: share “good” work publicly as a beacon; share “bad” work inside a private, earnest community that’s an “alchemical pot” for growth. By 2025, it basically resolves into the meme-able endpoint (@yacineMTB): “better to write something shitty and half baked than not at all.” Why care: it’s a real-time map of how a harsh productivity sermon turned into a practical system—make things, publish enough to matter, and use community to metabolize the ugly drafts—without pretending ambition is mandatory for everyone.
